title: From field to piecrust, heritage grains make a comeback
text:
From field to piecrust, heritage grains make a comeback
Interest in locally sourced grains is pushing rising demand for heirloom wheat varieties.
The land is shaped like a perfect slice of pie. It was the first thing Nancy Vail and Jered Lawson noticed nearly 25 years ago when they saw an aerial photo of the 14-acre triangular parcel of land they purchased with friend Karen Heisler along U.S. Highway 1.
They knew they had to call it Pie Ranch after its unique physical shape.
After all, the trio hoped to grow and raise on the land everything one would need to bake a pie. Berries and pumpkin for fillings. Cows for the butter. Chickens for the eggs. Lastly, and perhaps most crucially, wheat for the flour that forms the piecrust.
For Thanksgiving, the Monitor takes a closer look at some of the pumpkin pie’s ingredients, including pumpkins, eggs, and flour, to discover what stories they might hold. Our California bureau chief reports from a farm overlooking the Pacific Ocean, which grows heritage wheat and processes it into flour – part of a nationwide shift toward local grains.
“The theme of pie lends itself to bringing people together around a dish that you normally share with other people,” Ms. Vail says. “And it also incorporates a lot of diverse ingredients. So there is diversity in the production of the landscape.”
The couple knew they didn’t want to plant commercial wheat. Instead, in 2005, they planted heritage varieties. Pie Ranch is a regenerative farm where Ms. Vail, Mr. Lawson, and their team of about 20 people educate their community and others about sustainable farming. Regenerative farming is an agricultural approach that restores soil health, boosts biodiversity, and captures carbon by mimicking natural ecosystems rather than depleting them.
Growing and milling heirloom grains at Pie Ranch is core to this mission.
They’re not alone.
After nearly a century of the U.S. market being dominated by a few types of white flour, ancient and heritage wheat varieties are making a resurgence. Across the country, small farmers are turning away from modern wheat and working to revive heritage grains. A 2017 study by Cornell University researchers and colleagues, published in the Journal of Cereal Science, documented growing demand for these long-forgotten varieties.
These heirloom varieties are prized for their complex flavor, high nutritional value, and resilience.
After Pie Ranch was established in 2002, Ms. Vail and Mr. Lawson planted white Sonora wheat – a soft white grain that was originally brought to California in the 16th century by Spanish missionaries. The grain became an important crop for Indigenous peoples and early Californians.
After purchasing the initial wedge of land, the couple acquired an additional 13 acres. They also lease about 400 acres at nearby Cascade Ranch where they grow a portion of their wheat.
Following some years of low yields and climate challenges with white Sonora wheat, Ms. Vail and Mr. Lawson pivoted in 2010 to growing India Jammu, a spring hard heirloom wheat that thrives in warm, Mediterranean-like climates with little irrigation, making it a resilient, climate-adaptive varietal.
The ranch, which offers panoramic views of the Pacific Ocean, serves primarily as an educational nonprofit organization helping to educate community members and budding farmers about regenerative farming. Also, the team grows and mills its own wheat at the farm, packaging the flour into brown paper bags and selling it to customers at the on-site farm stand or online. The ranch crew also makes pies for its farm stand, placing them in a glass enclosure where they also sell pastries and other baked goods. Most, if not all, ingredients are sourced from the ranch.
Wheat production at Pie Ranch is small – just about 2,000 pounds during this year’s harvest. Much of what they grow is sold at the farm stand in small batches. Companion Bakeshop, in nearby Santa Cruz, purchases some of their wheat to create a specialty loaf they sell to customers.
During the 20th century, a commercial food production boom squeezed out small wheat farmers, leaving the crop dominated by massive commodity farms on the Great Plains.
It also led to the proliferation of modern commercial wheat varieties, which tend to have shallow roots and rely heavily on synthetic fertilizers and pesticides to garner high volumes. In contrast, heritage grains possess deep, expansive root systems.
Mr. Lawson says he’d like to produce more wheat to meet the needs of the community, but there are several challenges in doing so. There is a severe lack of specialized harvesting equipment made for smaller wheat producers, he says. Most wheat production equipment – from the storage bins to mills – are made for larger producers.
And then there’s the weather. Mr. Lawson says they are concerned about this year’s predicted increased rains thanks to El Niño, a tropical Pacific climate pattern that weakens trade winds, shifts jet streams, and can increase the risk of flooding.
“With El Niño we’re probably going to get more rain than we probably want,” Mr. Lawson says. “That’s a challenge for wheat production. If it rains and it doesn’t stop, it can drown the plants.”
Since hosting their first group of high school students more than 20 years ago, more than 1,000 youngsters and 4,000 members of the public have visited to learn about regenerative farming and cooking at the ranch. During these visits, the Pie Ranch team teaches the “seed to table” process, specifically using wheat to show how grains fit into a regional food system.
The Pie Ranch team also trains other farmers in San Mateo County to grow wheat as part of its wider focus on regenerative agriculture and diversified grain cultivation.
Through its Cascade Regenerator Program, new farmers learn how to manage crop planning, which includes planting and monitoring diversified crops like India Jammu wheat and barley.
“We want other farmers to grow their own wheat, too,” Mr. Lawson says.
Their dream, the couple say, is for people to abandon the generic flour in the grocery aisles. Instead, they hope, some day soon, several small farmers in the area will grow enough wheat to sustain and feed their own communities.
